answer.rationale: Both declining metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the top of the self-serve funnel, and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a fix there can plausibly move both. memory_86 and memory_31 are the two load-bearing records for that choice, so they are what I spend the verification budget on: memory_86 because it is the direct match to the observed onboarding decline, and memory_31 because 'cutting required fields' is exactly the kind of intervention whose headline lift can be an artifact of measuring activation rather than revenue. That is the downstream risk I am flagging: fewer signup fields means less qualifying data, which can degrade lead routing and pipeline quality even while activation counts rise — and memory_44 says enterprise value here comes through sales-assisted paths that depend on that qualifying data. Neither onboarding memory reports retention or revenue outcomes, unlike memory_73 which does; that asymmetry is a reason to treat the 'durable lift' claim as unconfirmed rather than settled. I am explicitly not choosing promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 records first-term renewals -12pp and labels it unsuitable for repeat use, so it buys new accounts against the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. referral_incentive (memory_57) is clean but targets established customers, not the segment that is actually bleeding. activation_messaging (memory_91) is my fallback if verification shows the onboarding records were activation-only or ran on a non-comparable cohort. Scale is a small guarded test with a true holdout and downstream instrumentation — qualified pipeline and first-term renewal, not just completion rate — because the inherited summaries are compressed and may have lost the very caveats that matter here.
